summary.text: Zooplankton are the plankton that must eat other organisms to live, ranging from microscopic protozoans to jellyfish.
They feed on phytoplankton, bacteria, other zooplankton and detritus, and in turn are food for higher consumers such as fish.
Though mostly carried by currents, many can move under their own power, for example to avoid predators through daily vertical migration.

facts.label: Crustacean members
facts.value: Copepods, krill, amphipods and ostracods, among others

facts.label: Disease link
facts.value: Crustacean zooplankton can harbour the cholera bacterium

items.prompt: How do tiny crustacean zooplankton help the bacterium that causes cholera survive in water?

options.label: It clings to their shells, which feed it
They carry it in their guts to land
They eat the bacteria's predators
Their waste warms the water for it

items.explain: Cholera bacteria attach to the chitin exoskeletons of crustacean zooplankton, which supply them with carbon and nitrogen.

items.prompt: The same species of tiny crustacean is raised in cold water and in warm water. Where do adults tend to end up larger?

options.label: In the warm water
In the cold water
They end up the same size
Whichever has more light

items.explain: Plankton are mostly ectotherms, which grow more slowly and mature at a larger body size in colder environments.

items.prompt: In spring, phytoplankton suddenly multiply. Why can zooplankton numbers catch up quickly?

options.label: They switch to making their own food
Fish stop feeding on them in spring
Being small, they respond fast
They drift in from the deep sea floor

items.explain: Because zooplankton are typically small, they can respond rapidly to increases in phytoplankton, as during the spring bloom.

items.prompt: Why are most zooplankton found in surface waters rather than the deep?

options.label: They need sunlight to photosynthesize
Deep water pressure crushes them
Deep water is too salty for them
That is where their food is plentiful

items.explain: Zooplankton cannot make their own food, so they gather in surface waters where phytoplankton and other zooplankton are abundant.

items.prompt: Mercury in seawater ends up concentrated in large fish. What part do zooplankton play in this?

options.label: They break mercury down into harmless salts
They are a key link passing it up the food web
They absorb it and lock it in the sea floor
They have no part, since fish skip them

items.explain: Zooplankton are a key link in the biomagnification of pollutants such as mercury, and they are food for higher consumers like fish.

items.prompt: Along a coast where deep water is pulled up to the surface, zooplankton gather in large numbers. What best explains this?

options.label: The rising water is warmer and calmer
Predators avoid the cold coastal water
Nutrients brought up boost their phytoplankton food
The rising water is less salty

items.explain: Mixing of the water column, such as upwelling, affects nutrient supply and so phytoplankton production, the main physical factor shaping where zooplankton live.

paragraphs.heading: Animal drifters
paragraphs.text: Zooplankton are the plankton that must eat other organisms to thrive. Their name comes from Greek words meaning "animal" and "drifter". Like all plankton, they cannot swim well against currents, so they are carried along in oceans, seas, lakes and rivers. Most are microscopic, but some, such as jellyfish, are big enough to see with the naked eye.

paragraphs.heading: Eaters, not makers
paragraphs.text: Phytoplankton can make their own food, often using sunlight, but zooplankton cannot. So zooplankton feed on other living things, such as phytoplankton, which are usually smaller than they are. Their menu includes bacteria, phytoplankton, other zooplankton, detritus (also called marine snow) and even swimming animals. Because their food is most plentiful near the top, zooplankton are found mainly in surface waters.

paragraphs.heading: A huge range of life
paragraphs.text: Many single-celled protozoans are zooplankton, including foraminiferans, radiolarians and some dinoflagellates. Important animal zooplankton include jellyfish and the Portuguese Man o' War; crustaceans like copepods, krill and amphipods; arrow worms; molluscs such as pteropods; and salps and larval fish. They feed in many ways, from filter feeding to predation to partnerships with phytoplankton, as seen in corals. Some spend their whole lives as plankton, while others drift for only part of their lives before becoming swimmers or settling on the sea floor.

paragraphs.heading: Blurry lines
paragraphs.text: In very small organisms, the line between making food and eating it often breaks down. Studies suggest that more than half of microscopic plankton are mixotrophs, which get energy and carbon both from plastids inside them and from outside sources. Many tiny zooplankton could therefore also be classed as phytoplankton.

paragraphs.heading: Patchy and on the move
paragraphs.text: Although currents carry them, many zooplankton can move on their own, to escape predators or to meet more prey. They are not spread evenly or randomly but gather in patches, as phytoplankton do. Some species are strictly limited by salinity and temperature, while others tolerate wide ranges. Breeding, predation, the amount of phytoplankton, and the mixing of the water column, which controls nutrients and so phytoplankton growth, all shape where they gather.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: By eating phytoplankton, zooplankton feed fish and other consumers higher up the food web and help package organic material into the biological pump. Being small, they can respond quickly when phytoplankton surge, as in the spring bloom. They also form a key link in the biomagnification of pollutants like mercury. Some even harbor disease: crustacean zooplankton can carry the cholera bacterium Vibrio cholerae on their chitin shells, which supply it with carbon and nitrogen.

paragraphs.heading: Size matters
paragraphs.text: Body size has been called a "master trait" for plankton, with a strong effect on growth, reproduction, feeding and death. Most plankton are ectotherms, which cannot make enough heat to warm themselves, so their body processes follow the outside temperature. In colder water they grow more slowly but mature at a larger size, a pattern called the temperature-size rule. The processes behind it are still unknown.
